cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: For a projectile launched at an angle $$\theta$$ above the horizontal, what is the vertical velocity at the highest point of its trajectory?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze vertical motion**
As the projectile rises, the downward acceleration of gravity decreases its upward vertical velocity component.  

**Step 2: Identify the peak condition**
At the highest point (peak), the object momentarily stops moving upward before starting to fall back down. Therefore, the vertical component of velocity must be:  
$$v_y = 0$$

**Step 3: Final Result**
The vertical velocity at the peak is **Zero**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Two projectiles are launched with the same initial speed at complementary angles (e.g., $$30^\circ$$ and $$60^\circ$$). How do their horizontal ranges compare?

options.A: The one launched at $$60^\circ$$ has a larger range.
options.B: The one launched at $$30^\circ$$ has a larger range.
options.C: They have the exact same range.
options.D: It depends on the mass of the projectiles.

cards.why:
**Step 1: Write range formula**
$$R = \frac{v_0^2 \sin(2\theta_0)}{g}$$

**Step 2: Compare sine arguments for complementary angles**
Let $$\theta_1 = \theta$$ and $$\theta_2 = 90^\circ - \theta$$.  
For $$\theta_2$$, the sine term is:  
$$\sin(2(90^\circ - \theta)) = \sin(180^\circ - 2\theta) = \sin(2\theta)$$

**Step 3: Compare range values**
Since $$\sin(2\theta_1) = \sin(2\theta_2)$$, the ranges are mathematically identical.

**Step 4: Final Result**
They have the **exact same range**.

cards.title: 1.1 Projectile Motion
body: **Projectile Motion** is a form of motion experienced by an object or particle (a projectile) that is thrown near the Earth's surface and moves along a curved path under the action of gravity only.

cards.title: 1.1 Projectile Motion — Deep Dive (1/2)
body: When an object is launched into space, it exhibits two independent, simultaneous one-dimensional motions: a horizontal motion with constant velocity (zero acceleration) and a vertical motion with constant downward acceleration due to gravity ($$g \approx 9.8\text{ m/s}^2$$). This independence of vertical and horizontal components is a cornerstone of classical mechanics, first systematically analyzed by Galileo Galilei.

The trajectory of a projectile is always parabolic in the absence of air resistance. The horizontal component of the velocity ($$v_x$$) remains constant throughout the flight because there are no horizontal forces acting on the projectile (neglecting air resistance). This means the horizontal acceleration ($$a_x$$) is strictly zero. Consequently, the horizontal displacement ($$x$$) is given by a simple linear equation: $$x = v_{0x} t = (v_0 \cos\theta_0) t$$.

Conversely, the vertical component of the velocity ($$v_y$$) is continuously modified by gravitational acceleration. The vertical acceleration ($$a_y$$) is constant and directed downwards, which is represented as $$-g$$ (or $$-9.8\text{ m/s}^2$$). This component behaves exactly like a freely falling body or an object thrown vertically upward, governed by the standard kinematic equations: $$y = (v_0 \sin\theta_0) t - \frac{1}{2}gt^2$$ and $$v_y = v_0 \sin\theta_0 - gt$$.

Why it matters: Understanding Projectile Motion is not only fundamental to athletic activities like kicking a football or launching a basketball, but it is also critical for engineering ballistic trajectories, launching satellites, and designing safety systems in aerospace engineering. The same principles dictate how packages dropped from planes land, requiring precise mathematical integration of horizontal and vertical vectors.

cards.title: 1.1 Projectile Motion — Deep Dive (2/2)
body: To mathematically describe the path, we can eliminate the time variable ($$t$$) from the parametric equations. By solving for $$t = \frac{x}{v_0 \cos\theta_0}$$ and substituting it into the vertical displacement equation, we derive the trajectory equation: $$y = (\tan\theta_0)x - \frac{g}{2(v_0 \cos\theta_0)^2}x^2$$. This quadratic relationship explicitly proves that the geometric path of a projectile is a parabola.

cards.title: 1.1 Projectile Motion — Comparative Analysis
body: Motion Component — Acceleration — Velocity Behavior — Governing Kinematics Equation | Horizontal ($$x$$) — $$a_x = 0$$ — Constant ($$v_x = v_{0x}$$) — $$x = v_{0x} t$$ | Vertical ($$y$$) — $$a_y = -g$$ — Uniformly changing ($$v_y = v_{0y} - gt$$) — $$y = v_{0y}t - \frac{1}{2}gt^2$$

> **💡 Did You Know?**: A bullet fired horizontally and a bullet dropped vertically from the same height at the exact same instant will strike flat ground at the same time, because their vertical motions are identical and independent of their horizontal speeds!

> **🧠 Pro-Tip**: In any projectile problem, always look for the 'time of flight' ($$t$$) first. Since time is a scalar, it is the fundamental bridge that connects the horizontal and vertical components of motion.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: What is the shape of the mathematical trajectory of an ideal projectile?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Write parametric equations**
$$x = (v_0 \cos\theta_0)t \implies t = \frac{x}{v_0 \cos\theta_0}$$
$$y = (v_0 \sin\theta_0)t - \frac{1}{2}gt^2$$

**Step 2: Eliminate time variable**
Substitute $$t$$ into the vertical equation:  
$$y = (\tan\theta_0)x - \left(\frac{g}{2v_0^2 \cos^2\theta_0}\right)x^2$$

**Step 3: Analyze the equation form**
This is in the quadratic form $$y = ax - bx^2$$, which defines a parabola.

**Step 4: Final Result**
The shape is a **Parabola**.

cards.title: 1.2 Circular Motion
body: **Circular Motion** is the movement of an object along the circumference of a circle or rotation along a circular path.

cards.title: 1.2 Circular Motion — Deep Dive (1/2)
body: Circular motion can be broadly classified into Uniform Circular Motion (UCM) and Non-uniform Circular Motion. In Uniform Circular Motion, the object travels along a circular path at a constant speed. However, because velocity is a vector quantity having both magnitude and direction, the velocity is continuously changing because its direction is constantly changing tangent to the circular path. This constant change in direction implies that the object is continuously accelerating.

This acceleration is called centripetal acceleration ($$a_c$$), meaning "center-seeking." It is always directed radially inward toward the center of the circular path, perpendicular to the linear velocity vector. The magnitude of centripetal acceleration is mathematically formulated as $$a_c = \frac{v^2}{r}$$, where $$v$$ is the constant speed and $$r$$ is the radius of the circle. Without this inward acceleration (and the corresponding centripetal force), the object would fly off along a straight-line tangent to the circle, obeying Newton's first law of motion.

In Non-uniform Circular Motion, both the speed and the direction of the object change. In this scenario, the acceleration vector has two perpendicular components: centripetal (radial) acceleration ($$a_c$$) which changes the direction of velocity, and tangential acceleration ($$a_t$$) which changes the magnitude of velocity (speed). The total linear acceleration ($$a$$) is the vector sum of these two: $$a = \sqrt{a_c^2 + a_t^2}$$.

Why it matters: Circular motion principles are vital for astronomical calculations, such as determining the orbits of planets and artificial satellites. They are also essential in everyday engineering, such as designing banked highways to prevent cars from skidding, manufacturing centrifuges for medical laboratories, and calculating the structural limits of high-speed roller coasters.

cards.title: 1.2 Circular Motion — Deep Dive (2/2)
body: When a car rounds a flat curve, the centripetal force is provided entirely by the static friction between the tires and the road surface. If this frictional force is insufficient ($$f_s < \frac{mv^2}{r}$$), the car slips outward. To mitigate this hazard, engineers bank roads at a specific angle $$\theta$$ so that the normal force contributes to the centripetal force, allowing safe transit even in low-friction conditions: $$\tan\theta = \frac{v^2}{rg}$$.

cards.title: 1.2 Circular Motion — Comparison of Circular Motion Types
body: Parameter — Uniform Circular Motion — Non-Uniform Circular Motion | Speed ($$v$$) — Constant — Variable | Tangential Acceleration ($$a_t$$) — Zero ($$a_t = 0$$) — Non-zero ($$a_t = \frac{dv}{dt}$$) | Centripetal Acceleration ($$a_c$$) — Non-zero ($$a_c = \frac{v^2}{r}$$) — Non-zero ($$a_c = \frac{v^2}{r}$$) | Total Acceleration Vector — Radial only ($$a = a_c$$) — Resultant ($$a = \sqrt{a_c^2 + a_t^2}$$)

> **💡 Did You Know?**: Astronauts orbiting the Earth are in a state of perpetual free-fall. They are moving horizontally at a speed so high ($$\approx 7.9\text{ km/s}$$) that as they fall toward the Earth, the Earth's surface curves away beneath them at the exact same rate, keeping them in a circular orbit!
> **🧠 Pro-Tip**: Centripetal force is not a new type of force; it is a label we apply to net physical forces (like tension, gravity, or friction) that act toward the center of a circular path.

$$a_t = \frac{dv}{dt}$$

**Step 2: Apply UCM conditions**
In Uniform Circular Motion, the speed $$v$$ is constant:  
$$v = \text{constant} \implies \frac{dv}{dt} = 0$$

**Step 3: Final Result**
Therefore, the tangential acceleration is **Zero**.

**Step 2: Analyze the velocity vector**

cards.title: 1.3 Relative Motion
body: **Relative Motion** is the calculation of the motion of an object with regard to some other moving or stationary reference frame.

cards.title: 1.3 Relative Motion — Deep Dive (1/2)
body: In the physical universe, there is no such thing as absolute rest or absolute motion. All motion measurements are inherently relative to a chosen frame of reference. A frame of reference is a coordinate system used to measure the position, velocity, and acceleration of an object. For example, a person sitting on a moving bus is at rest relative to the bus, but moving at $$60\text{ km/h}$$ relative to an observer standing on the roadside.

To mathematically formulate relative velocity, let us consider two objects, $$A$$ and $$B$$, moving relative to the ground (fixed frame $$G$$). The velocity of $$A$$ relative to $$B$$ (denoted as $$\vec{v}_{AB}$$) is given by the vector subtraction: $$\vec{v}_{AB} = \vec{v}_{AG} - \vec{v}_{BG}$$ (or simply $$\vec{v}_{AB} = \vec{v}_A - \vec{v}_B$$). This equation shows that the relative velocity of $$A$$ with respect to $$B$$ is the velocity of $$A$$ minus the velocity of $$B$$.

When dealing with motion in two dimensions, we must employ vector addition. For instance, if a boat attempts to cross a flowing river, its resultant velocity relative to the riverbank ($$\vec{v}_{bg}$$) is the vector sum of the boat's velocity relative to the water ($$\vec{v}_{bw}$$) and the water's velocity relative to the bank ($$\vec{v}_{wg}$$): $$\vec{v}_{bg} = \vec{v}_{bw} + \vec{v}_{wg}$$. This vector addition can be resolved into orthogonal components using trigonometric functions.

Why it matters: Relative motion calculations are essential for navigation. Pilots must continuously adjust their heading to account for wind speed and direction (wind drift) to stay on their planned flight path. Similarly, maritime vessels must calculate the effects of ocean currents, and radar tracking systems must calculate relative velocity to intercept incoming targets.

cards.title: 1.3 Relative Motion — Deep Dive (2/2)
body: In classical mechanics, these transformations are known as Galilean transformations. They assume that space and time are absolute, meaning time passes at the same rate in all frames of reference. While this holds true for everyday speeds, Einstein's theory of Special Relativity reveals that at speeds approaching the speed of light, relative velocity calculations must be modified because time and space are no longer absolute.

cards.title: 1.3 Relative Motion — Relative Velocity Scenarios (1D and 2D)
body: Physical Scenario — Vector Equation — Magnitude Calculation | Collinear (Same Direction) — $$\vec{v}_{AB} = \vec{v}_A - \vec{v}_B$$ — $$v_{AB} = v_A - v_B$$ | Collinear (Opposite Directions) — $$\vec{v}_{AB} = \vec{v}_A - (-\vec{v}_B)$$ — $$v_{AB} = v_A + v_B$$ | Perpendicular (2D) — $$\vec{v}_{AC} = \vec{v}_{AB} + \vec{v}_{BC}$$ — $$v_{AC} = \sqrt{v_{AB}^2 + v_{BC}^2}$$

> **💡 Did You Know?**: When rain falls vertically, it appears to hit the windshield of a moving car at an angle. This is because the velocity of the rain relative to the car is the vector difference between the rain's vertical velocity and the car's horizontal velocity!

> **🧠 Pro-Tip**: When writing relative velocity subscripts, keep the order consistent: $$\vec{v}_{AC} = \vec{v}_{AB} + \vec{v}_{BC}$$. Notice how the inner subscripts ($$B$$) 'cancel' out, leaving you with the outer subscripts ($$A$$ and $$C$$).

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: What is the SI unit of torque (moment of a force)?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Write torque formula**
$$\tau = F \cdot d \cdot \sin\theta$$

**Step 2: Identify units of parameters**
Force $$F$$ has unit Newton ($$\text{N}$$).  
Distance $$d$$ has unit meter ($$\text{m}$$).  
Sine of an angle is dimensionless.

**Step 3: Combine units**
$$\text{Unit of } \tau = \text{N} \cdot \text{m} = \text{N}\cdot\text{m}$$

**Step 4: Final Result**
The SI unit is **$$\text{N}\cdot\text{m}$$**.

cards.q: An object moves in a circle of radius $$r$$ with constant speed $$v$$. If the radius is halved while keeping the speed constant, the centripetal acceleration becomes:
cards.why:
**Step 1: Write centripetal acceleration formula**
$$a_{c1} = \frac{v^2}{r}$$

**Step 2: Substitute the new radius**
Let the new radius be $$r' = \frac{r}{2}$$. The new acceleration $$a_{c2}$$ is:  
$$a_{c2} = \frac{v^2}{r'} = \frac{v^2}{r/2} = 2 \left(\frac{v^2}{r}\right)$$

**Step 3: Establish relationship**
$$a_{c2} = 2 a_{c1}$$

**Step 4: Final Result**
The acceleration is **Doubled**.

cards.title: 1.4 Moment of a Force
body: **Moment of a Force** (or torque) is a measure of the tendency of a force to cause a body to rotate about a specific point or axis.

cards.title: 1.4 Moment of a Force — Deep Dive (1/2)
body: Just as a net force is required to change the linear motion of an object (producing linear acceleration), a net moment of a force (or torque) is required to change the rotational motion of an object (producing angular acceleration). The point about which the object rotates is called the pivot, fulcrum, or axis of rotation.

The magnitude of the moment of a force depends on two primary factors: the magnitude of the applied force ($$F$$) and the perpendicular distance from the axis of rotation to the line of action of the force. This distance is called the moment arm or lever arm ($$d$$). Mathematically, the torque ($\tau$, Greek letter tau) is defined as: $$\tau = F r \sin\theta$$, where $$r$$ is the distance from the pivot point to the point of application of the force, and $$\theta$$ is the angle between the force vector and the position vector. The SI unit of torque is the Newton-meter ($$\text{N}\cdot\text{m}$$).

According to the convention of rotational mechanics, counter-clockwise moments are designated as positive ($$+$$), while clockwise moments are designated as negative ($$-$$). A body is said to be in complete mechanical equilibrium when two conditions are met: the net external force is zero (translational equilibrium: $$\sum \vec{F} = 0$$), and the net external torque about any axis is zero (rotational equilibrium: $$\sum \vec{\tau} = 0$$). This second condition is known as the **Principle of Moments**.

Why it matters: The principle of moments is the bedrock of civil engineering and architecture. It dictates how bridges support heavy loads, how skyscrapers withstand wind forces, and how cranes lift immense loads without tipping over. It is also the operational mechanism behind simple machines like crowbars, pliers, scissors, and the human skeletal-muscular system.

cards.title: 1.4 Moment of a Force — Deep Dive (2/2)
body: When a heavy load needs to be balanced, the positioning of the pivot is crucial. For a uniform rod balanced at its center of gravity, any weights placed on either side will create rotational tendencies. By applying $$\sum \tau = 0$$, we can find unknown weights or distances: $$W_1 d_1 = W_2 d_2$$. This simple equation allows a small force applied at a large distance to balance a massive weight at a short distance, which is the definition of mechanical advantage.

cards.title: 1.4 Moment of a Force — Factors Influencing Torque ($$\tau = F d$$)
body: Factor — Physical Change — Effect on Rotational Tendency | Force Magnitude ($$F$$) — Increasing $$F$$ — Increases torque proportionally | Lever Arm ($$d$$) — Increasing distance from pivot — Increases torque proportionally | Angle of Application ($$\theta$$) — Approaching $$90^\circ$$ (perpendicular) — Maximizes torque ($$\sin 90^\circ = 1$$) | Angle of Application ($$\theta$$) — Approaching $$0^\circ$$ or $$180^\circ$$ (parallel) — Reduces torque to zero ($$\sin 0^\circ = 0$$)

> **💡 Did You Know?**: Archimedes famously boasted about the power of levers, stating: "Give me a place to stand on, and I will move the Earth." He understood that with an infinitely long lever and a suitable pivot, any force, no matter how small, could generate enough torque to move any mass!

> **🧠 Pro-Tip**: When calculating moments, always identify the pivot point first. Choosing a pivot point where an unknown force acts is a clever mathematical trick because it reduces the torque of that force to zero ($$r = 0$$), simplifying your equilibrium equations.

cards.why:

In physics and engineering, we adopt standard coordinate rules for rotational quantities.

**Step 2: Match directions to signs**

Clockwise (CW) rotations are defined as **negative** ($$-$$).

**Step 3: Final Result**

cards.why:
**Step 1: Write torque formula**
$$\tau = F \cdot r \cdot \sin\theta$$

**Step 2: Analyze conditions for zero torque**
For a non-zero force ($$F \neq 0$$):
- Either $$r = 0$$ (force applied at the pivot).
- Or $$\sin\theta = 0 \implies \theta = 0^\circ \text{ or } 180^\circ$$ (force parallel to the lever arm).

**Step 3: Relate to physical behavior**
Both conditions describe a line of force that passes directly through the pivot point, making the perpendicular lever arm length $$d = 0$$.

**Step 4: Final Result**
Torque is zero **when the line of action of the force passes directly through the pivot point**.

tips.text: A projectile is any object that is given an initial velocity and then moves under the effects of gravitational force and air resistance.
Projectile motion can be analysed as two separate motions in the horizontal and vertical directions.
If air resistance is ignored, the horizontal motion is motion with uniform velocity.
The vertical motion is uniformly accelerated motion with uniform downward acceleration. It is the same as for a body falling vertically under the action of gravity.
Can an object have a constant speed but a changing velocity?
Give examples of objects that move in a circular path.
When a particle moves along a curved path: 4. a) Can it have constant speed? b) Can it have constant velocity? c) What happens to the direction of the particle’s motion?
Is motion along a circular path uniform or accelerated?
How does the velocity of an object change?
Since velocity is a vector quantity, it has both magnitude and direction. Therefore, the velocity changes when either its magnitude or its direction, or both magnitude and direction, change.
Motion in two dimensions & moments: Horizontal: x = vₓ t | vₓ constant Vertical: vᵧ = v₀ᵧ − gt ; y = v₀ᵧ t − ½gt² (up positive). Time of flight links the two.
Formula: Moment = F × perpendicular distance Equilibrium: clockwise moments = anticlockwise about the same point. Units N·m.

is a form of motion experienced by an object or particle (a projectile) that is thrown near the Earth's surface and moves along a curved path under the action of gravity only.
Zero acceleration ($$a_x = 0$$): the velocity stays constant ($$v_x = v_{0x}$$), so $$x = v_{0x}t$$.
Constant downward acceleration ($$a_y = -g$$): $$v_y = v_{0y} - gt$$ and $$y = v_{0y}t - \frac{1}{2}gt^2$$.

A bullet fired horizontally and a bullet dropped vertically from the same height at the exact same instant will strike flat ground at the same time, because their vertical motions are identical and independent of their horizontal speeds!
In any projectile problem, always look for the 'time of flight' ($$t$$) first.
